title: India Ramps Up Ebola Screening as WHO Declares Africa Outbreak a Global Emergency. What NRI Travellers Need to Know.
excerpt: With over 300 suspected cases and nearly 90 deaths in the DRC and Uganda, India’s health ministry activates airport surveillance — and the diaspora’s travel plans face a new variable.
body:
On Sunday, May 17, the World Health Organisation declared the Ebola outbreaks in the Democratic Republic of the Congo and Uganda a Public Health Emergency of International Concern — its highest level of alarm. By Monday, India’s health ministry had convened a review meeting, activated screening protocols, and put the National Centre for Disease Control on heightened alert.

No case of Ebola has been reported in India. But for the millions of NRIs who transit through African airports, visit East African business hubs, or have family connections across the continent, the declaration introduces a practical complication to travel planning that warrants attention rather than panic.

## What Is Happening in Africa

The current outbreak involves the Bundibugyo strain of Ebola, a rarer variant with a case fatality rate of roughly 30 per cent — lower than the more notorious Zaire strain’s 60-90 per cent, but still extraordinarily dangerous. As of mid-May, the WHO has counted over 300 suspected cases and nearly 90 confirmed deaths across the DRC and Uganda, with cases confirmed in major cities including Kinshasa and Kampala.

Cross-border transmission is the WHO’s primary concern. The DRC shares borders with nine countries, and population movements through conflict-affected regions make containment difficult. A US healthcare worker who contracted the virus in the DRC is currently receiving treatment in Germany. The WHO has stopped short of calling this a pandemic but warned the outbreak could be “much larger” than currently documented.

## India’s Response

India’s preparedness draws on lessons from its COVID-19 experience. The NCDC is monitoring developments in real time, coordinating with international health agencies, and maintaining surveillance at international airports with direct or connecting flights from affected regions. Dr. Sanjay Rai from AIIMS Delhi has publicly assessed India’s risk as low, but emphasised the importance of awareness among healthcare workers and proper infection control protocols.

Former WHO Chief Scientist Soumya Swaminathan suggested India could extend medical support to affected regions, leveraging its pharmaceutical manufacturing capacity and experience with infectious disease containment. India produces a significant share of the world’s generic medicines and vaccines, and any future Ebola vaccine manufacturing could involve Indian facilities.

The Indian health ministry’s review meeting assessed screening mechanisms, laboratory readiness, and response strategies for a potential suspected case. Under India’s One Health framework, coordination spans human health, animal health, and environmental surveillance — a structure that health officials say positions the country better than it was during the 2014 West African Ebola crisis.

## What NRIs Should Know

For diaspora members with travel to East or Central Africa, the practical implications are immediate. Airport screening in India will likely involve thermal scanning and health declaration forms for passengers arriving from or transiting through affected countries. The US Centers for Disease Control has issued travel advisories for the DRC and Uganda, and several European nations are increasing border health checks.

Ebola spreads through direct contact with the blood, body fluids, or tissues of infected individuals — it is not airborne. This means the risk to casual travellers is genuinely low, but anyone visiting healthcare facilities, attending funerals, or working in close contact with local populations in affected areas should take heightened precautions.

The larger context matters too. The United States withdrew from the WHO under the Trump administration earlier this year, which public health experts say may limit American access to the real-time infectious disease intelligence that proved critical during previous outbreaks. For Indian health authorities — and for the diaspora navigating a complex global health landscape — the WHO’s emergency declaration is both a warning and a call to maintain the surveillance infrastructure that kept Ebola out of India during every previous outbreak.

India’s health ministry has not imposed travel restrictions. The WHO explicitly advised against border closures, noting they tend to impede the movement of health workers and supplies more than they prevent viral spread. But awareness, screening, and preparedness have quietly moved up a notch — and NRI travellers transiting through Africa would be wise to do the same.
